definitions.meaning: to reserve a seat or passage is to buy it in advance
reading matter: volumes on a shelf

explanation.surface: Someone buys a train ticket to the town of Reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading is a town west of London, so the surface reads as a rail journey; the capital R hides the plain sense of reading matter.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb for reserving a seat; the other is the plural noun for printed volumes you read.

parts.note: a billy goat is the horned male goat
a cock is a feathered male bird

explanation.surface: A hat decorated with horns and feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: The billycock is a round felt hat, a bowler; the clue builds it from two farmyard males.
explanation.definitionFit: A billycock is a hard round felt hat, much like a bowler.

parts.note: a street musician who turns a handle on a barrel instrument is a grinder of this kind

explanation.surface: A loud machine for milling coffee or meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grinder' suggests a mill, but it is the street musician turning a barrel instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The barrel instrument cranked by a street musician gives its name to that grinder.

parts.note: a skinflint is a miser who would skin a flint, so his harvest would be pebbles

explanation.surface: A miser chooses what to grow for the cheapest possible harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: A skinflint is so mean he would skin a flint, a stone; so his harvest would be a stone crop, which is also a succulent wall plant, sedum.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedum, the low succulent of walls and rockeries, is named for growing on stones.

definitions.meaning: a heliograph signals with sunlight, so answering one is returning the light signal
a sudden recollection of a past scene, as in a film cutting to earlier events

explanation.surface: A signaller with a mirror answers and asks whether you recall the code.
explanation.definitionFit: Signalling with mirrors means sending light straight back; the film sense is a scene returning to earlier memories, hence 'remember?'.

parts.note: fall is the American word for autumn, the season of bonfire night
Guy Fawkes, burned in effigy every November in Britain

explanation.surface: Guy Fawkes is the seasonal scapegoat, burned each autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonfire Night, 5 November, is when Britain burns effigies of Guy Fawkes, plotter against Parliament in 1605; it falls in autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe who takes the blame for others, a stooge or patsy.

parts.note: a train coming in to the station has got there, and someone successful has also got there

explanation.surface: An official steps up to the speaker's dais as successor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeeded to' suggests inheriting an office; read differently, a train that reaches the platform has reached its goal, as a successful person has made it.
explanation.definitionFit: To have made it in life is to have got there, as a train does at the platform.

clue.text: After aspiration love in this cottage breaks down

parts.note: aspiration is the breathy sound of the letter H

indicators.note: the word love collapses and its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A romance in a little cottage falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the rearranged LOVE (giving OVEL) behind H.
explanation.definitionFit: A hovel is a poor, mean dwelling, a run-down cottage.

parts.note: a disc jockey plays records, but this man keeps records, documents in a collection

explanation.surface: A record collector insists he is not a disc jockey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Records' tempts you to think of discs; it means documents kept in an archive.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeper of historical documents, the man in charge of an archive's papers.

definitions.meaning: music set in a particular key, written in notes
the mistress of a house carried its keys on a chain at her waist

explanation.surface: A lady of the castle is mentioned in passing.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece written in a tonality is so set; a housekeeper with her bunch of keys hanging at her belt is furnished likewise.

clue.text: Record great wave — a mutually advancing one

parts.note: a ship's log is its record of a voyage
a roller is a long heavy ocean wave

explanation.surface: A surfer logs a huge wave, helped along by a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Logrolling is the American term for politicians trading favours, each pushing the other's measure forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A politician who trades votes or praise so that each side advances the other's cause.

definitions.meaning: the wartime French government that worked with the German occupiers sat at this spa town
a mineral water bottled from the springs of that French town

explanation.surface: A traitor is denounced alongside a bottle of spa water.
explanation.definitionFit: The French town gave its name both to the wartime regime that cooperated with Germany and to its bottled spring water.

clue.text: Charlotte that there mother of Titans

parts.note: yon is the old or dialect word for 'that over there'
Ge, or Gaia, is the earth goddess of Greek myth who bore the Titans

explanation.surface: A rustic voice points out a woman called Charlotte as the mother of giants.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte Mary Yonge was a popular Victorian novelist, author of The Heir of Redclyffe.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Charlotte M. Yonge is identified by her forename alone.

clue.text: Tenure of a sort that follows the hammer

indicators.note: the word for sort comes after the word for the hammer in the answer

parts.note: a gavel is the small hammer of an auctioneer or chairman
kind means sort or type

explanation.surface: A form of land holding is sold off when the auctioneer's hammer falls.
explanation.walkthrough: Gavelkind was a Kentish custom of land tenure dividing an estate equally among sons.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old system of holding land, a kind of tenure under English law.

clue.text: Lord Rye would not be himself as this officer

indicators.note: a man not being himself is out of sorts, so the letters of his name are put in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A nobleman acts out of character when serving as an officer.
explanation.definitionFit: An orderly officer is the one on daily duty in a regiment, and the word alone names that duty officer or attendant.

clue.text: Then, in France, a flower for the races

parts.note: donc is French for then or therefore
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A Frenchman then pins on a flower to go to the races.
explanation.walkthrough: Doncaster in Yorkshire holds the St Leger, one of England's classic horse races.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire town is a major horse-racing venue, host of the St Leger meeting.

definitions.meaning: lively and stylish, full of dash
someone fair at ironing moves the iron quickly over cloth, making rapid strokes

explanation.surface: A lively laundress is praised for her ironing.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirited means bold and lively; a quick ironer makes swift strokes across the cloth.

parts.note: a leather belt and strap worn by officers is named after the Victorian general who devised it

explanation.surface: A rigidly conservative military commander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidebound' means narrow-minded, but read literally it is bound with hide: General Sir Sam Browne gave his name to the officer's leather belt.
explanation.definitionFit: General Sir Sam Browne invented the cross-strapped leather belt that bears his name.

parts.note: Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, divinities to be worshipped, contended for the golden apple judged by Paris

explanation.surface: A few charming women sell apples at market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adorable' means fit to be adored, as divinities are; the apple is the golden one Paris awarded to Aphrodite.
explanation.definitionFit: Female deities are beings to be adored, and three of them fought over Paris's golden apple.

clue.text: Monarch has the point of being indispensable

parts.note: a king is a monarch
a pin has a sharp point

explanation.surface: A king is told that his sharpness makes him vital to the realm.
explanation.definitionFit: The essential bolt on which a mechanism turns stands for the one indispensable person or thing.

clue.text: To do so may be fun, Lily, but nothing comes of it

indicators.note: the letters may be rearranged into another word, so the two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: Fooling around with Lily may be enjoyable but leads nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To do so' looks like a definition but is a link; 'may be' signals the anagram of FUN and LILY.
explanation.definitionFit: To cancel or make void means that the effort is undone and leaves no result.

clue.text: Tried at this or just tried

definitions.text: Tried at this or just tried

parts.words: Tried at this or just tried
parts.note: putting 'at' in front gives a word meaning tried; alone the word means tried in the old sense of tested by temptation

explanation.surface: Someone either had a go or was merely put to the test.
explanation.walkthrough: The Biblical sense of being tried, as when Abraham was tested, is to be led into temptation; prefix 'at' and you get the ordinary word for tried.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lured toward wrongdoing is being tested, the old sense of tried.

clue.text: Export from East to U.S.S.R. perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps tells us the letters are only a possible arrangement, to be reordered

parts.note: the abbreviation for the Soviet Union, taken as its letters

explanation.surface: Goods travel from the East to the Soviet Union, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: TO and USSR rearranged make TUSSOR, with E added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Tussore is a coarse silk from wild Indian silkworms, exported from the East.

definitions.meaning: old lists of names to be prayed for, read aloud in church
a snapped string of pearls sends its beads rolling across the floor

explanation.surface: A broken necklace scatters while someone draws up registers.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval prayer lists of the dead were called this; read as two words it pictures beads rolling off a broken string.

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: return means turning back, so the second word of the pair is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's whole world comes back to them.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Our Mutual Friend, John Rokesmith marries Bella Wilfer; she is his be-all. 'in return' turns ALL into LLA after BE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rokesmith's beloved in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend is Bella Wilfer, the heroine he marries.

definitions.meaning: to push up the price at auction by bidding
travelling to the capital is going up, wherever you start from

explanation.surface: A man makes an offer before heading for the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you always go 'up' to London, so a quick trip there is a run up.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising the price with bids is one sense; a quick trip to the capital is another, since travel there is always 'up'.

clue.text: Flighty female form of old stiff collar

definitions.text: Flighty female form of old stiff collar

parts.words: Flighty female form of old stiff collar
parts.note: a ruff is both a pleated Elizabethan collar and a wading bird; the flighty female is the hen of that bird

explanation.surface: A frivolous woman wears an old-fashioned starched collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' sounds like a character judgement but means able to fly: the female ruff, a sandpiper, has its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: The hen of the ruff, a wading bird, is given a separate name from the male.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the surname goes round the numeral

parts.note: Jane Eyre, heroine of Charlotte Bronte's novel
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Plain Jane is described as one up on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homely' looks like plain, but refers to a home: an eagle's nest, high 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle's nest is a bird's home perched high up, so the definition points to a lofty dwelling.

parts.note: dog followed by the name of the classical tongue means corrupt, ungrammatical use of it

explanation.surface: Someone swears at their dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog Latin' is a mock or debased Latin; the clue looks like cursing at a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: The classical tongue of Rome, when debased, is called dog-something, so the bad language goes with dog.

parts.note: Wellington was nicknamed the Iron Duke, and factories are works, so an industrial version of him is a metal plant

explanation.surface: A town called Wellington goes industrial.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duke of Wellington was known as the Iron Duke; his deeds, his works, become a foundry.
explanation.definitionFit: A factory where metal is smelted or forged shares the Iron Duke's nickname plus 'works'.

clue.text: A hero type wrecked the, plant

indicators.note: a wreck is a thing broken apart, so the letters of the three words are rebuilt

explanation.surface: A heroic type destroyed the factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' could be a factory, but it is the botanical sense: an air plant, growing without soil.
explanation.definitionFit: An epiphyte or air plant draws moisture from the air rather than from soil.

clue.text: Gets 'flattened at times when shadows fall

definitions.meaning: makes level or smooth, as in levelling the ground
poetic plural for evenings, when the light fades

explanation.surface: Something is knocked flat at dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb for making flat or level; the other is the poetic word for evenings, when the sun sinks.
